1.pericope_label: The two and a half tribes dismissed with charge and blessing

schools.summary: Gill sets the discharge in its circumstances — the promise fulfilled, the land for the most part subdued, the war ended, rest on all sides, and the nine tribes and a half quietly settled — and reports the Jewish reckoning of fourteen years, seven in subduing the land and seven in dividing it. Calvin presses the difficulty that the enemy still held part of the land whose possession should have ended the war, and answers that Israel's own sloth in drawing back from God's proffered help dissolved the obligation; he praises the two tribes and a half for waiting quietly to be sent for, finds the point of Joshua's charge in its permanence, since he frees them from temporary service only to bind them for ever as soldiers of the one true God and names the law of Moses lest they drift into airy speculations, and holds that the men who stayed behind could not honestly have claimed a share of the spoil, Joshua exhorting liberality rather than enforcing a legal right and asking not an equal partition but enough to remove all cause of envy.

Henry sees a prudent general disbanding an army that never meant to make war its trade and sending it home to beat swords into ploughshares; he cites the best chronologers for six or seven years of service and thinks it probable that in winter quarters some of the men slipped over Jordan to see their families, sending others in their room while the quota of forty thousand stood ready. He ranks the commendation under readiness of obedience, constancy of adherence, and faithfulness to the divine law, taking the last to mean that they had kept up religion in their part of the camp, a rare thing among soldiers; and he notes that the counsel Joshua gives is not political but pious, saying nothing of fortifying cities or enlarging territory.

Clarke puts the war at seven years and infers that the men never once revisited their homes, though only the river lay between the camp and their inheritance and it was fordable at every season but harvest; he expounds Joshua's charge clause by clause, the commandment for moral precept and the law for rite and ceremony, cleaving as a union never to be dissolved, and argues that without an affectionate filial attachment to the Maker duty would be irksome and impossible. On the spoil he thinks the share plainly due to those who defended the families and tilled the ground, without whom the rest could not safely have left home. Wesley reduces commandment and law to two words for one thing, and agrees that the men who stayed had a claim, while denying the portions were equal.

Keil and Delitzsch read the commended clause narrowly, as observing what had to be observed with respect to the commandment, and set the repetition about Manasseh's two halves down to the copious breadth of early Hebrew historical style.

debates: How long the service lasted and whether the men went home in the interval. Henry allows six or seven years and thinks some slipped over Jordan during winter quarters with substitutes in their room; Clarke allows seven and holds that they never once revisited home although the ford was easy; Gill and Calvin both report the Jewish figure of fourteen years.

Whether the discharge came too early, the land not being wholly possessed. Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that Israel's own sloth in refusing what God was ready to bestow released the two tribes and a half from their bargain; Gill simply describes the land as for the most part subdued.

Whether the tribes who stayed behind had a claim on the plunder. Calvin denies any legal claim and reads Joshua's words as an exhortation to liberality calculated to remove envy; Clarke treats the share as plainly due to the men who guarded the families and worked the ground; Wesley grants the claim but denies the portions were equal.
outliers: Henry's reading of the commended phrase as keeping the keeping, and his remark that religion kept up in a part of the camp is a rare and excellent thing among soldiers.
Keil and Delitzsch's explanation of the chapter's repetitions as a feature of early Hebrew historical style rather than a fault.
Calvin's account of the discharge as an exchange of temporary service for permanent enlistment under God.
themes: spoil divided with those who stayed

10.pericope_label: The altar at Jordan, and the embassy from Shiloh

schools.summary: Gill reads the Geliloth of the border as the meanders and turnings of the river near Jericho, and distinguishes the iniquity of Peor as a single act from an altar built for continuance. Calvin allows that nothing was farther from the builders' intention than to innovate, yet holds they sinned not lightly in attempting a novelty without any regard to the high priest and in a form very liable to be misconstrued, drawing from it the apostle's rule that one must attend not only to what is lawful but to what is expedient; he then defends the vehemence of the western tribes, since a second place of sacrifice would profane the worship and open a door to superstition, and still grants that their zeal was not free from turbulent impetuosity in making ready for war before inquiring.

Henry weighs the opinion that the altar stood on the Canaan side so the builders might see the figure of the Shiloh altar across the water, but prefers their own side, asking what they had to do to build on another man's land without consent and noting that no suspicion would have arisen otherwise. He allows the motive entirely, as a care to keep hold of Canaan's religion and a bridge of fellowship, while faulting the discretion, since a thing with an appearance of evil should have been referred to the oracle or explained to their brethren beforehand; he calls the western tribes' suspicion excusable and their prudence in sending to inquire no less commendable; and he says plainly of the charge that it is well they were not able to make it good, while praising the closing offer of land as the spirit of Israelites indeed.

Clarke insists the west bank can never be meant, being neither their territory nor of any use to their own people for worship, and dwells with Henry on the offer by which the western tribes would straiten themselves rather than let their brethren feel the want of an altar. Wesley repeats almost word for word the argument that the altar stood on the builders' own side, and grants that God had pardoned the national punishment of Peor while the blot and the corrupt leaven still remained.

Ellicott prefers the eastern bank and finds in the description a reminder of the very thing the altar was to enforce, that both borders of Jordan belong to the promised land, while noting a proposed site twenty miles north of Jericho on the western bank; he insists the text means the altar, a copy of the one altar given to Israel for sacrifice, set up so the eastern tribes might appeal to it as proof that they too were the people of Jehovah; and he finds in the whole scene the strongest proof of the narrative's antiquity, since no writer of Jeremiah's day could have conceived a single rival altar to Jehovah as cause for war. Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the chapter's two descriptions of the site by taking Canaan in a restricted sense that stops at the Jordan valley, and answer that the plague had already avenged the guilt of Peor.

debates: Which bank the altar stood on. Henry, Wesley, Clarke and Ellicott all settle on the eastern side, Henry and Wesley on the ground that men do not build on another's land and that no suspicion would otherwise have arisen, Clarke on the uselessness of a western altar to eastern worshippers, Ellicott on the sense of the phrase; Ellicott alone records a western site that has been proposed, and Keil and Delitzsch resolve the difficulty in the wording instead by restricting the name of Canaan.

Whether the builders were at fault. Henry allows the motive and faults only the discretion, thinking they should have consulted the oracle or forewarned their brethren; Calvin makes the omission a real though not a heavy sin, chiefly in slighting the high priest and choosing a form open to misconstruction.

Whether the muster for war was proportionate. Calvin defends it as an illustrious display of piety while conceding turbulent impetuosity; Henry calls the suspicion excusable and stresses the prudence of inquiring first; Ellicott treats the readiness to fight as evidence of how seriously the law was then held.
outliers: Ellicott's argument from the scene to the antiquity of the narrative, against dating the requirements it presupposes to the age of Jeremiah.
Calvin's application of the apostle's distinction between the lawful and the expedient to a monument built with good intentions.
Henry's remark on the indictment, that it is well the accusers were not able to make it good.

21.pericope_label: The answer of the eastern tribes

schools.summary: Calvin makes the restraint of the reply a rule for imitation, that when a thing rightly done is falsely blamed it may be enough to refute the censure only so far as clears oneself; he says the state of the case turns on a definition, notes that strictly God cannot be set above other gods since there are none to compare him with and that the phrase is framed to the common sense of ordinary men, and meets the objection that the law forbids such erections by distinguishing images meant to represent God, which are condemned, from a heap of stones raised as a trophy or memorial, which is nowhere prohibited — otherwise Joshua and many holy judges after him would have defiled themselves. Gill reads the repeated names as steadiness of faith and vehement affection for the truth, and goes behind the builders' fear to its premise, granting that Jordan was the eastern border of Canaan strictly so called while insisting that the land beyond it was no less promised to Abraham, since the Amorites driven out of it were Canaanites too.

Henry finds the reply fair and ingenuous, since the accused neither retort the charge nor upbraid their brethren with the injustice of their threatenings nor demur to their jurisdiction, but give a soft answer that turns away wrath. He describes the fear for posterity as arising only on the journey home, finds in the text a word signifying great perplexity of mind, and traces the danger exactly: distance and the river would keep the eastern children from the yearly feasts until they were reckoned inconsiderable members of the church and at last none at all, the western children monopolizing the privileges of the altar in their pride while the eastern ceased from fearing the Lord. From this he draws the rule that the form and profession of godliness may be kept without the life and power, but the life and power will not long be kept without the form.

Clarke thinks the manner of the answer as creditable as its matter, since men conscious of their innocence let Phinehas finish a discourse composed of little else than accusations, and he wishes some public assemblies of his own day that lay claim to the highest refinement would take the lesson; he calls the heaped divine names exceedingly emphatic and hardly translatable, coming nearest in Luther's rendering, holds that nothing but the utmost consciousness of integrity could have induced men to add the imprecation that follows, and says the altar served no religious purpose but testified that the tribes were one people under one constitution. Wesley reads the repetition as zeal, and finds in the closing clause a sudden apostrophe to God such as vehement speech runs into.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the three divine names heaped together — the strong one, the Supreme Being to be feared, and the truly existing covenant God — and note that the invocation is strengthened further by repeating all three. Ellicott insists that the structure is the pattern or copy of the altar of Jehovah rather than an altar of its own, proving the eastern tribes' equal right to approach him; he traces the taunt the builders feared through Ephraim's abuse of the Gileadites to Jeroboam's calves, and applies the case to his own day, wishing that the altars still occasioning dispute could be known to be, like this one, not for sacrifice but for a witness.

debates: Whether the law's prohibitions touched such a structure at all. Calvin raises the difficulty and answers that only images representing God are forbidden, memorial heaps being everywhere allowed; Clarke observes that the builders' express disclaimer of sacrifice is what keeps the altar clear of the law; Ellicott resolves it in the wording, since the text calls it the altar, a copy, rather than an altar.

What weight the heaped divine names carry. Keil and Delitzsch read them as a formal strengthening of the oath; Clarke as untranslatably emphatic and evidence that the creed was unchanged; Gill as steadiness of faith; Wesley as zeal and earnestness; Calvin alone qualifies the phrase itself as an accommodation to common speech.

Whether the fear for posterity was well founded. Henry treats it as a just foresight and builds a rule about the means of grace upon it; Calvin approves it as timely provision for their children; Gill quietly undercuts its premise by insisting the eastern land was always part of the promise.
outliers: Clarke's aside that public assemblies of his own day claiming the highest refinement might learn manners from the Reubenites.
Ellicott's application of the case to contemporary disputes about altars, wishing they could be known to be witnesses rather than places of sacrifice.
Henry's maxim that you take away grace if you take away the means of grace.
themes: three names heaped in an oath
children shut out in time to come

30.pericope_label: The explanation accepted, and the altar named

schools.summary: Calvin praises Phinehas and the ambassadors for tempering their zeal and admitting the excuse willingly, and makes the case a warning against the obstinacy of men who, once offended, can be appeased by no defence and find something to carp at rather than seem to yield to reason; from their acknowledgment that Jehovah is in the midst of them he infers that no one revolts from God unless God has first abandoned him, and that we persevere in piety only so far as he sustains us by his hand. Gill supposes the name of the altar to have been inscribed or engraved upon it, so that its purpose might be known in time to come.

Henry credits the peaceful issue to a disposition for peace on both sides matching the zeal on both sides, remarking that quarrels about religion, for want of wisdom and love, often prove the fiercest and hardest to make up. He lists what the ambassadors refrained from doing — questioning the sincerity of the protestation, upbraiding the builders with a rashness that had cost an embassy, or fishing for evidence to make good a charge once made — and observes that the altar was left standing though it might as easily occasion idolatry in time as prevent it, the strong bearing the infirmities of the weak, with the single precaution of recording the explanation in a name.

Clarke reports the Targum's paraphrase, in which the majesty of the Lord dwells among them and the trespass would have been against the Word of the Lord, and finds in the conclusion a promise that a God present as the sole object of worship will abide as protector and portion; he notes that the name of the altar is absent from the common Hebrew editions and supplied in italics by the translators, though found in several manuscripts and in the Syriac and Arabic and necessary to the sense; and he closes with an excursus distinguishing true schism, a rent in apostolic doctrine and practice, from mere dissent from human institutions, condemning separation over non-essentials and holding that Christians who cannot think alike may agree to disagree without indifference. Wesley makes the deliverance a matter of prevention, since one who prevents an approaching mischief delivers as truly as one who removes it after it has fallen.

Keil and Delitzsch give Phinehas's testimony plainly, that because the eastern tribes had not been unfaithful the Lord was known to be among them and Israel was preserved from his judgments, and treat the closing clause as at once a name for the altar and its own explanation. Ellicott observes that the best token of the divine presence among men is the divine likeness in men, and takes the confession to be that Jehovah is God of all the twelve tribes alike.

debates: What it means that the eastern tribes delivered Israel out of the hand of the Lord. Henry reads it as a denial, that they had not after all delivered Israel into his hand; Keil and Delitzsch as preservation from judgments already threatened; Wesley as a deliverance by prevention, which he holds as real as a deliverance by cure.

Whether the altar should have been allowed to stand. Henry notes that it might as easily occasion idolatry in time as prevent it, and reads the forbearance as the strong bearing the infirmities of the weak; Calvin is content that the naming of it was enough to draw the people off from superstition.

The text of the altar's name. Clarke observes that the word is missing from the common Hebrew editions and supplied in italics, defending it from manuscripts and the Syriac and Arabic; Gill assumes without question that it was inscribed on the altar itself; Keil and Delitzsch read the whole clause as name and explanation together.
outliers: Clarke's excursus distinguishing schism from dissent, with his conclusion that Christians who cannot think alike may agree to disagree and let each go to heaven his own way.
Wesley's maxim that he who prevents an approaching mischief delivers a man as truly as he who removes it after it has fallen.
Calvin's inference that idolatry always presupposes a prior abandonment by God, so that perseverance is his sustaining and not our own.
themes: a name that is its own explanation
